As far as I can tell with respect to Hume and the PSR, he has a simple way of rejecting it. In Hume's day, the universe was taken to be infinite. Hume has no problem with an infinite contingent series.

Russell and Mackie took up Hume's ideas with regard to skepticism about the necessary, mostly in the forms of Compositional Fallacy, i.e. there is no reason that the logic or laws operating over the universe's parts need apply to universes as such. We can stop at accepting the universe as simply brute fact, and only treat the things which we can know about its parts a posteriori. Moreover, that there is no analytic truth to be had about worlds themselves.

This appears to be supported by the related argument that once you can explain everything in a world, what you have done is just explain that world. In other words, the mistake is categorical - treating the universe as an object or event in the regular sense is a mistake. Rather, the world is just what we find to be inside it. Therefore, while the PSR could be applied to things which come to exist in a world, it need not apply to the world - if the PSR held for all contingent facts in an infinite universe, then there is just an ending series of relations going back for time unending.

The real trouble, of course, is modern cosmology, which traces all facts in the universe backward to a Planck-sized entity, that is at some point in time non-partitive.
